\chapter{Things You Ask For}
\label{ch:hi-ask-for}
\hlchaptermodality{45}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five everyday things I might ask someone for in Hindi, and say which of them came down from Sanskrit and which walked in with Persian.}

Complete HI-C45-soap and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[phal]{\hi{फल} (phal) — a fruit}

\label{lesson:HI-C45-fruit}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{parivār} mean, and what did \emph{log} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{फल}}
\textbf{\hi{फल}} (\emph{phal}) — \textquotedblleft{}a fruit\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{phala}, which named the fruit on the tree and, in the same breath, the result of anything you did. Hindi still carries both senses: the mango in your hand and the outcome of a year's work take the same word.

English readers meet the second sense in translations of the Gita, where \textquotedblleft{}the fruit of action\textquotedblright{} is a word-for-word rendering rather than a figure the translator reached for. The Persian layer of Hindi later brought \emph{mevā} for dried fruit and nuts, so the orchard and the shop shelf can be named separately — an inherited word and a borrowed one dividing the work between them, which is a habit worth watching for.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things you might ask someone for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{phal}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{phal}, then \emph{log}, so the new one sits beside the last one you learned
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{फल} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a fruit\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kapṛā]{\hi{कपड़ा} (kapṛā) — cloth}

\label{lesson:HI-C45-cloth}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{phal} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{कपड़ा}}
\textbf{\hi{कपड़ा}} (\emph{kapṛā}) — \textquotedblleft{}cloth\textquotedblright{}.

The plain, unceremonious word: the bolt on the shelf, the washing on the line, the shirt on your back. Behind it is Sanskrit \emph{karpaṭa}, a rag or a patched garment, and the \hi{ड़} in the middle is what a thousand years of ordinary speech did to that \emph{-ṭ-} caught between two vowels.

Beside it Hindi keeps \emph{vastra}, lifted from Sanskrit untouched, which turns up on a wedding invitation rather than over a washing line. Two words, one meaning, and the register telling them apart.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: a fruit and a cloth.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kapṛā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{phal}, then \emph{kapṛā}, and ask for each with \emph{kṛpayā} in front
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{कपड़ा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}cloth\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dīyā]{\hi{दीया} (dīyā) — an oil lamp}

\label{lesson:HI-C45-lamp}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kapṛā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{दीया}}
\textbf{\hi{दीया}} (\emph{dīyā}) — \textquotedblleft{}an oil lamp\textquotedblright{}.

A small clay lamp with a wick floating in oil — the kind lit in rows along a wall at Diwali. Behind it is Sanskrit \emph{dīpa}, 'lamp', on the root \emph{dīp-}, 'to blaze'.

The \emph{p} softened away in everyday speech and left \hi{दीया} behind, while the formal \emph{dīpak} kept it. Diwali is that same \emph{dīpāvalī}, 'a row of lamps', worn down in the same direction: the lamps are still in the name of the festival, only harder to see.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: a fruit, a cloth, and a lamp.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dīyā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dīyā}, then \emph{kapṛā}, so the two objects sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{दीया} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}an oil lamp\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[namak]{\hi{नमक} (namak) — salt}

\label{lesson:HI-C45-salt}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{dīyā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{नमक}}
\textbf{\hi{नमक}} (\emph{namak}) — \textquotedblleft{}salt\textquotedblright{}.

Persian \emph{namak}, taken whole, and one of the plainest examples of Hindi's second inheritance. The word that came down from Sanskrit is \emph{lavaṇa}, and it survives mostly in careful writing and in chemistry, while the borrowed word does the cooking.

Persian salt also handed Hindi a measure of character: \emph{namak-halāl} is someone true to the salt they have eaten at your table, and \emph{namak-harām} is the one who is not. A pantry word doing moral work.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and one of them is not a thing you can hold.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{namak}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{namak}, then \emph{dīyā}, then \emph{kapṛā}, backwards down the run
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{नमक} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}salt\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sābun]{\hi{साबुन} (sābun) — soap}

\label{lesson:HI-C45-soap}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{namak} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{साबुन}}
\textbf{\hi{साबुन}} (\emph{sābun}) — \textquotedblleft{}soap\textquotedblright{}.

Arabic \emph{ṣābūn}, reaching Hindi through Persian — and behind the Arabic sits Latin \emph{sāpō}, which the Romans had themselves borrowed from their northern neighbours, who used the stuff on their hair before anyone used it for washing.

So the word went north to south, south to east, and arrived here. English \textquotedblleft{}soap\textquotedblright{} and \hi{साबुन} are the same ancient word arriving by two different roads, one short and one very long.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: a fruit, cloth, a lamp, salt, soap.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sābun}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{phal}, \emph{kapṛā}, \emph{dīyā}, \emph{namak}, \emph{sābun}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
